name: Self-reversing screw
summary: A screw cut with a right-hand and a left-hand groove joined at the ends drives a shoe to and fro at constant speed while it turns one way.

ratio.typical: one lead per turn (48 mm by default); stroke = lead x (turns per traverse - turn-round), 120 mm over 3 turns

topology.notes: ground, screw (revolute in its pillow blocks), carriage (prismatic on its guide), shoe (revolute pivot in the carriage); the shoe in the groove is a form-closed cam contact; counted mobility 2, because the shoe's swivel on its pivot is set by the groove's walls, which the count does not see

explain.motion: The screw carries a right-hand and a left-hand groove of the same lead, joined at both ends into one endless track that crosses itself twice on every turn. A shoe rides the groove on a pivot in the carriage. Turning the screw one way at a steady speed carries the shoe along at a steady 48 mm per turn. Near each end the groove bends round within 1 turn of the screw: the shoe slows, stops, swivels across into the other groove and comes back, so the carriage runs 120 mm there and back every 6 turns with the screw never changing direction.
explain.forces: The groove's wall pushes on the side of the shoe, and the push along the screw is the turning effort over the lead, less friction. At the pitch radius the grooves lean 28.6° from the circumference, so the shoe swivels through 57.2° at each turn-round. Where the grooves cross, the shoe loses its walls in the middle and is carried by its two ends, which is why it must be longer than a crossing.
explain.benefits: Turns steady one-way rotation into a steady to-and-fro with no reversing gear, clutch or change of direction, and the reversal points are cut into the screw, so they never drift.
explain.limits: The stroke and the reversal points are fixed when the screw is cut. The sharp points where the grooves cross and the long shoe wear fastest, and a worn shoe can turn into the wrong groove and reverse early; heavy loads wear the shoe quickly.

build.ground: base with the screw's two pillow blocks and a straight guide for the carriage along the screw
build.defining_relations: Both grooves have the lead p = 48 mm; at the pitch radius rp = 14 mm the lead angle is atan(p / (2 pi rp)) = 28.6°. Over each traverse of N = 3 turns the shoe moves by the trapezoidal law: steady at one lead per turn, with a parabolic turn-round of tr = 0.5 turn at each end (blend tr / N = 1/6), so the stroke is h = p (N - tr) = 120 mm and the track repeats after 2N = 6 turns. The shoe lies along the groove: its swivel is the change of atan(s' / rp), plus or minus 28.6° in the steady runs. Groove 7 mm wide and 4 mm deep; at the lead angle a crossing is 7 / sin(57.2°) = 8.3 mm long along the groove, bridged by a shoe 18 mm long.
build.notes: Screw axis horizontal, the shoe on the near side, seen in front elevation where the grooves cross in a diamond pattern. The track is cut by Manifold in pieces along the law, the root turned back as one core. The shoe's blade is an ellipse in plan, its underside cut round the screw's axis; it swivels on a pivot bolt in the carriage's upright.

groove.centreline: x = s(theta) at the pitch radius, theta over 6 turns: right hand out, left hand back
groove.make: boolean: the track cut in pieces of the groove's section along the law, the root turned back as one core

joints.note: at is the shoe's centre at the pitch radius Rp (mid-depth of the groove); the track's centre line runs along the axis by the law over 2N turns, so it crosses itself

params.note: turns of the screw per traverse
turn-round at each end, turns of the screw

review.note: New record, reviewed against its kinematics before the build (#255). Six phases of the solved cycle (every 60 degrees of the cycle, one turn of the screw): the shoe at mid-stroke on a crossing, 48 mm further, at the far end turning round (swivel through 0 to -57.2), and back the same way; the shoe's travel against the screw's turn is an exact triangle wave with rounded tips, 24 mm per half turn in the steady runs. Decided: 3 turns per traverse and a turn-round of half a turn either side of each end, so the cycle is 6 turns, the shoe runs steady for 2 of every 3 turns and the turn-round is a sixth of the cycle, long enough to watch with no time map; lead 48 on a 32 mm screw, a lead angle of 28.6 degrees at the 14 mm pitch radius, so a crossing is 8.3 mm long and an 18 mm shoe bridges it with 4.8 mm in the groove at each end; the reference at mid-stroke, where both grooves cross under the shoe, so the opening drawing shows the shoe bridging a crossing. Default view FRONT, the screw's near side where the grooves cross in diamonds and the shoe lies along its groove at true size. One tick per screw turn on the shoe's trace, a fixed one-lead dimension above it and the stroke dimension between the posed ends, so a turn reads as one lead; plot of the shoe's position against the screw's turn (the triangle wave over 6 turns); a detail view at the crossing under the shoe at the reference. The carriage is drawn see-through on purpose (teaching.seeThrough): its upright stands in front of the shoe in FRONT. Controls: the screw's turn only; the lead, turns and turn-round are built into the screw, so they are not offered.

name: Rack-and-pinion stroke doubler
summary: A pinion carried on a slide rolls on a fixed rack and drives a free rack on its far side twice as far as the slide moves.

ratio.typical: output stroke = 2 x carrier stroke for any pinion; 160 mm for an 80 mm carrier stroke

topology.notes: ground with the fixed rack, carrier (prismatic on the ground), pinion (revolute on the carrier), free rack (prismatic on the ground); two gear meshes, the pinion with each rack

explain.motion: A carrier slides back and forth with a pinion turning on its axle. The pinion meshes a fixed rack on one side and a free rack on the other. As the carrier moves, the pinion rolls along the fixed rack, so its contact there stands still for an instant: it is the instant centre. The far side of the pitch circle is twice as far from that point as the axle, so it moves twice as fast: the free rack moves 160 mm while the carrier moves 80 mm, the same way, whatever the pinion's size.
explain.forces: The free rack's load comes back through the pinion on both sides: the carrier pushes with twice the output force, half of it taken by the fixed rack, so the stroke doubles and the force halves. The pressure angle of each mesh pushes the racks away from the pinion, and their guides take it.
explain.benefits: Doubles a short stroke in a narrow space with an exact, positive drive, and the 2:1 holds for any pinion, since only the rolling sets it.
explain.limits: The backlash of two meshes adds up at the output, and the racks must stay parallel over the whole stroke or the pinion binds. The carrier needs twice the output force, and the ratio cannot be changed.

build.ground: base with the fixed rack screwed and dowelled to it, a slide for the carrier and a slide for the free rack, all along x
build.defining_relations: The pinion (module 3, 16 teeth, pitch radius r = 24 mm) rolls on the fixed rack's pitch line: for a carrier travel x it turns θ = -x / r. The free rack meshes it on the opposite side, 2r from the fixed pitch line, and moves x - r θ = 2x, whatever r is. Carrier stroke 80 mm (±40), free rack stroke 160 mm (±80), pinion turn 191° over the stroke (80 / 24 rad).
build.notes: Seen in plan: the fixed rack below the pinion's centre, teeth up, the free rack above, teeth down. Relative to the carrier each rack moves ±40 mm, so 16 teeth (150.8 mm) keep both in mesh over the stroke. The carrier is the driven slide; the free rack rides its own slide from its back, its toothed side open for the pinion.

joints.note: the pinion rolls on the fixed rack: relative to the carrier the rack moves r per radian of the pinion's turn
the free rack on the pinion's far side: relative to the carrier it moves the carrier's travel again

params.note: module of the pinion and both racks
pinion pitch radius, m z / 2: half the distance between the racks' pitch lines

review.note: New record (#257), reviewed against its kinematics before the build and again on the six phases of the finished build. Six phases (every 60 degrees of the cycle): the carrier at -40, -20, +20, +40, +20, -20 mm and the free rack at -80, -40, +40, +80, +40, -40 mm, always twice the carrier and the same way; the pinion turns back as it rolls forward, +95.5 to -95.5 degrees (191 over the stroke, 80 / 24 rad); its contact with the fixed rack stays on the fixed pitch line under the axle. Decided: the carrier is driven by the linear drive along its own slide (standard section 8), not by Brown's crank and rod, so the lesson is the two straight strokes alone with no second mechanism in front of it; module 3, 16 teeth (pitch radius 24), a carrier stroke of 80 mm and a free rack stroke of 160 mm; both racks 16 teeth, enough to stay in mesh over the stroke; the carrier 84 mm long, so it shows past the pinion at both ends; the fixed rack drawn as frame (role frame) and the free rack as the output, so which rack moves reads at a glance. Default view PLAN (opened at 28 degrees), where the pitch circle, both pitch lines and both strokes show true. Traces: a mark on the free rack's pitch line (the comet) and the axle, both ticked every 30 degrees of the cycle, so at every tick the rack's step is twice the carrier's; overlays: the fixed pitch line, a circle at the instant centre, the line from it through the axle to the far contact (speeds 0, v, 2v), and the two stroke dimensions between the posed ends. Plot of the free rack against the carrier (a straight line of slope 2). Controls: the input only; the pinion size is not offered (the parts are built for one pinion), and the claim that the ratio holds for any pinion is the law, checked by the block's test at three radii. No section or detail view: the principle lies in plain view. No time map.

name: Chain stroke doubler
summary: A chain anchored to the frame runs round a sprocket on a moving carrier to an output slide, which moves twice as far as the carrier.

ratio.typical: output stroke = 2 x carrier stroke for any sprocket; 160 mm for an 80 mm carrier stroke

topology.notes: ground, carrier (prismatic on the ground), sprocket (revolute on the carrier), output (prismatic on the ground); four chain strands, each a higher pair: two chains, each with an anchored strand and a running strand. Overconstrained by two: the second chain repeats the first's relation the other way round, which is why the pair is tensioned against each other at one anchor

explain.motion: A carrier slides back and forth with a sprocket turning free on a stud. A roller chain is anchored to the frame, runs along under the sprocket, round its end and back over it to the output slide. When the carrier moves, the anchored strand grows by the carrier's travel, so the strand on the other side of the sprocket must shrink by the same amount: the chain runs round the sprocket and its far end moves twice as far, the same way. The output moves 160 mm while the carrier moves 80 mm, at twice its speed at every point of the stroke.
explain.forces: The sprocket is the moving pulley of a block and tackle, driven at its centre instead of at the rope: the output's load pulls the running strand, the anchored strand holds the same tension, so the carrier pushes with twice the output force. A chain only pulls, so a second chain round the other side of the sprocket, anchored at the frame's other end, pulls the output back.
explain.benefits: Doubles a stroke with one driven slide and no second drive, positively and exactly, and the doubling holds for any sprocket size, since only the anchored strand sets it.
explain.limits: Each direction needs its own chain, and the two must be kept tight against each other; chain stretch and slack at the anchors show twice at the output. The carrier needs twice the output force, and the ratio cannot be changed.

build.ground: base with the carrier's slide, the output's slide beside it, and an anchor block for each chain's held end, one at either end of the base
build.defining_relations: The sprocket (ISO 606 08B, 12 teeth, seat circle radius 24.53 mm) takes 152.4 mm of chain per turn, so r = z p / 2π = 24.26 mm. Each chain's anchored strand is held: for a carrier travel x the sprocket turns θ = -x / r, and the strand on its far side moves x again relative to the carrier, so the output moves x - r θ = 2x, whatever r is. Carrier stroke 80 mm (±40), output stroke 160 mm (±80), sprocket turn 189° over the stroke (80 / 24.26 rad).
build.notes: Seen in plan: the anchored strands run under the sprocket's centre (y -24.53), the running strands over it (y +24.53), the output slide beyond them. Chain A, in the sprocket's lower row, wraps its +x half: anchored at x -114.3, pinned to the output at -76.2. Chain B, in the upper row 16.5 mm higher, wraps the -x half: anchored at +114.3, pinned to the output at +76.2. Both 21 links, a whole number of pitches from each end to the sprocket, so a roller sits in a seat at both tangent points. Each chain end is pinned to an anchor bolt; the nuts on the bolts set each chain's length, the two chains drawn tight against each other.

params.note: chain per radian of the 12-tooth sprocket, z p / 2π

review.note: New record (#258), reviewed against its kinematics before the build. Six phases (every 60 degrees of the cycle): the carrier at -40, -20, +20, +40, +20, -20 mm and the output (chain A's end) at -80, -40, +40, +80, +40, -40 mm from its reference, always twice the carrier and the same way; the sprocket turns back as the carrier goes forward, +94.5 to -94.5 degrees (189 over the stroke, 80 / 24.26 rad); the anchored strands' ends stay where they are while the strand under the sprocket grows and shrinks, and the strand over it runs at twice the carrier's speed. Decided: the carrier is driven by the linear drive along its own slide (standard section 8), the output on a slide of its own beside it, so the two straight strokes lie side by side in plan as in the rack-and-pinion doubler; two chains, one per direction, since a chain only pulls and the drive works both ways: chain A wraps the sprocket's +x half and pulls the output out, chain B the -x half and pulls it back, in two rows of one sprocket so the four strands lie on two lines in plan, both anchored strands under the sprocket's centre and both running strands over it; a 12-tooth ISO 606 08B sprocket and chains of 21 links, a carrier stroke of 80 mm and an output stroke of 160 mm, the same strokes as the rack doubler so the two pages compare; the output a plain bar, the sprocket a link (it is an idler), the carrier the driver. Default view PLAN (opened at 28 degrees), where both strand lines and both strokes show true. Traces: chain A's end on the output (the comet) and the axle, both ticked every 30 degrees of the cycle, so at every tick the output's step is twice the carrier's; overlays: the line through both anchors (the anchored strands, at rest), a circle at the instant centre where the held strand leaves the sprocket, the line from it through the axle to the running strand (speeds 0, v, 2v), and both stroke dimensions between the posed ends. Plot of the output against the carrier (a straight line of slope 2). Controls: the input only; the sprocket size is not offered (the chains are built for one sprocket) and the claim that the doubling holds for any sprocket is the law, checked by the strand block's fixture test at three radii. No section or detail view: the principle lies in plain view. No time map.

name: Walking-beam transfer
summary: A beam on two equal cranks lifts every part off its notches, carries it one station on and sets it down, then returns empty below the rails.

ratio.typical: one station per crank turn: pitch = 2 x crank radius along the notch line

topology.notes: a parallelogram four-bar: ground, two equal cranks and the beam, count includes ground. The balls are carried by contacts that change from notch to seat and back each turn, so the mobility is not counted from them: one input moves everything.

explain.motion: Two equal cranks turn together, so the beam pinned to them translates round a 40 mm circle without turning. On the upper half of the circle its seats rise through the notches of the fixed rails, lift every ball at once, carry it one station on and set it down in the next notch; on the lower half the beam returns empty below the rails. Each turn moves every ball 38.4 mm along and 11.2 mm up the notch line, and each ball stands still in its notch for half of every turn while the cranks keep turning. The last ball rolls off onto the return track, and the packed queue on it rolls on one ball each turn, so the front ball is waiting in the first notch when the beam comes up under it.
explain.forces: The beam carries the whole row at once, so the crank torque is greatest while it lifts and small on the empty return. The balls are handed over at the ends of the circle's diameter, where the seats move nearly square to the notches, so nothing slides in a notch; but the beam moves fastest there, so each ball is picked up and set down at full crank speed.
explain.benefits: Every part moves the same distance at the same moment and is located in a notch between moves, so the pitch is exact and the parts never rub on each other or on the rails. One rotary input drives the whole row.
explain.limits: The parts are set down while the beam is still moving, so heavy or fragile parts need a drive that slows near the hand-over, such as a lift-and-carry drive with a rectangular path. The parallelogram passes its change points at the hand-overs, where both cranks lie along the line of their centres, so a real machine ties the two cranks by a chain or gears.

build.ground: the base, the two notched rails, the return tracks and the crank bearings
build.defining_relations: beam translation = crank pin displacement (two equal cranks of radius r, parallel and in phase); the hand-overs are the ends of the circle's diameter along the notch line, so one turn carries a ball 2r along the line: pitch 2r cos a and rise 2r sin a with r = 20 mm and sin a = 0.28; carry on the upper half turn, rest on the lower; every ball moves one slot of the closed circuit per turn
build.notes: The notch line rises so that the return can run back by gravity: the beam lifts each ball one rise per station and the return track gives the height back. The return runs beside the transfer, not under it: a return under the beam would have to climb back past the beam's own depth and travel, more than the beam can lift. The thirteen balls are like, so after one turn each stands where the next one stood and the picture repeats; the parallelogram is held on its parallel branch through the change points at 0 and 180 degrees.

review.note: T2 review 2026-10-27, six phases drawn from the solved motion at 0, 60, 120, 180, 240 and 300 degrees in VIEW -25 30: keep. Drive: two equal cranks (circular translation) rather than a lift-and-carry drive: one rotary input with the standard motor and belt (section 8), and the beam's whole motion is one closed curve to trace; the flat carry and square hand-over of a lift-and-carry drive are named in the limits. The notch line rises (sin a = 0.28) so the hand-overs lie at the ends of the circle's diameter: the seats meet the notches 16.3 degrees from square, inside the 45 degree flank of the V, so nothing slides, and the beam lifts each ball 11.2 mm per station, the height the gravity return gives back. Closed circuit: the return under the transfer was set aside, since a ball returning under the beam must climb back past the beam's depth and its fall below the rails, more than one seat can lift. The return runs beside the transfer: the out-track rolls the ball from the top notch across onto the return lane, a packed queue rolls down the lane and back across on the in-track, and the front ball rolls into the first notch while the beam is down. Every slot advances one per turn, so after one turn each ball stands where the next one stood (kin.bodies next, K2) and the loop shows no jump. Balls rather than pins: they roll across onto the cross tracks and round the corners, which a pin cannot. Trace: the seat at S2 draws the beam's 40 mm circle with 30 degree ticks; overlays: the notch line, the station (2r) and the crank radius; plot: a ball's advance (a step) against the beam's travel (a sine), the stepwise advance against the continuous motion. Solve checks: advance 38.4 mm and rise 11.2 mm per turn, circle 40 mm, dwell 180 degrees, all within tolerance. The parallelogram's change points fall at the hand-overs: held on the parallel branch as in the parallelogram linkage; a chain or gear tie between the cranks is an open question.

name: Hobson's joint
summary: Rods bent at a right angle slide in bores of two discs on shafts at 90°, so the output turns exactly with the input, with no gears.

ratio.typical: 1:1 exactly at every instant, round the fixed angle the rods are bent to (90° here)

topology.notes: ground, input and output discs on their revolutes, three bent rods each held by two cylindrical joints (one leg in a bore of each disc); counted mobility -4: the joint is overconstrained, since the count does not see that every leg is held parallel to its shaft and that all the bores lie on one radius; it moves with 1 degree of freedom

explain.motion: Each shaft ends in a disc with three bores on a 22 mm circle, the same in both. Three rods bent at 90° pass through the bores, one leg in each disc, each leg parallel to its own shaft. A leg can only slide and turn in its bore, so a rod never turns: it is carried round, its corner keeping to the plane that bisects the right angle, and the two discs are held at the same angle. The output turns at exactly the input's speed at every instant, and each leg slides 44 mm out and back in its bore on every turn.
explain.forces: Torque passes as the push of each leg on the side of its bore, 22 mm from each axis, and the rods carry it round the corner in bending. The legs slide in their bores while they carry the load, so the sliding friction is the joint's loss.
explain.benefits: Constant velocity round a right angle with no gears and no cross: two drilled discs and a few bent rods, and it drives either way.
explain.limits: The shaft angle is fixed by the bend of the rods and cannot change. The legs slide under load, so the joint binds when the bores are not true, wears in its bores and suits low speeds and light torque. One rod, or two set opposite each other, would not do: twice a turn it can carry the output on backwards, so three or more are spaced round the circle.

build.ground: base with two pillow blocks under each shaft, the shafts level and at a right angle, their axes meeting at J
build.defining_relations: Bores on one radius r = 22 mm in both discs; rods bent to the shafts' angle beta = 90°. A rod's corner B lies on its input bore line and r from the output axis. With B - J = x a1 + q (q square to the input axis a1), x = (q · a2) / (1 - cos beta) on the assembled root, so at 90° x = q · a2: the corners keep to the plane through J that bisects the right angle, and output angle = input angle exactly. Each leg slides r cos(theta) from mid-stroke, a stroke of 2r = 44 mm per turn. The other root, x = -(q · a2) / (1 + cos beta), turns the output the other way; it meets the assembled one where q · a2 = 0 (the rod's bores straight above or below the shafts), twice a turn for each rod. Rods at 0°, 120° and 240° reach those points one at a time, so the other two hold the output on its root.
build.notes: Shafts level at 55 mm, the input along x and the output along y, their axes meeting at J; discs Ø64 x 12 with their front faces 56 mm from J; rods Ø6 with 94 mm legs and a 6 mm bend radius, the bores through, so each leg's end comes out behind its disc as it slides. review.note: New record, reviewed against its kinematics before the build (#256). Six phases of the solved cycle (input 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300): rod 1's corner runs (22, 22, 0), (11, 11, 19), (-11, -11, 19), (-22, -22, 0), (-11, -11, -19), (11, 11, -19) from J, an ellipse in the plane x = y that bisects the right angle; the rods never turn; each leg slides 44 mm in its bore, the corner farthest from both discs at 0 and nearest at 180, both legs of a rod together; speed ratio 1 within 1e-4, output minus input 0, K1 residual 1e-14. Branch: the other root of a rod's corner (x = -q · a2) turns the output the other way and meets the assembled root where the rod's bores stand straight above or below the shafts (input 90 and 270 for rod 1); solved for all three rods, the other root gives each rod a different output turn, so it cannot be taken while the other two hold the output, and the rods reach their switch points one at a time, 60 degrees apart. Two rods set opposite would reach theirs together and could not hold it, so three rods at 120 degrees. Decided: bores on a 22 mm circle in Ø64 discs 36 mm from J, a stroke large enough to see against the disc; the reference with rod 1 in the plane of the shafts, so the section in that plane cuts both its legs along their bores. What must be seen: equal angles on both shafts, by a mark on each disc's face at the same angle traced with ticks every 30 degrees (the same twelve ticks on both); rod 1's corner traced with the comet; the corners' plane as a line; the leg stroke as a dimension between its posed ends; why the angle is fixed, by the shaft angle arc beside the rod's bend arc, both 90 degrees. Both discs see-through on purpose (teaching.seeThrough) so the legs show in their bores. Default view VIEW 135 30. Controls: the input only; the shaft angle is fixed by the bend of the rods, so it is not offered. Looked at again on the finished build (record view, PLAN, SIDE, the 28° view, the section and the explode, both sheets): keep. The view from the outside corner of the right angle replaced ISOMETRIC, where the output disc stood in front of the rods' corners; there both discs face the viewer at 45° with their arrows and ticks side by side and the three bends in front; the corner's trace lies edge-on in it (its plane holds the line of sight) and reads in SIDE and the 28° view. The discs moved from 36 to 56 mm from J, so they come off their shaft ends in the explode without meeting and more of each sliding leg shows between disc and corner; a raised index arrow on each disc at the same angle.

name: Wobble box
summary: A turning shaft with an inclined journal nods a trunnioned ring, which rocks an output shaft at right angles to and fro through the journal's angle.

ratio.typical: output swing ±α, the journal's angle to the shaft (±15° here); arm stroke 2 L sin α

topology.notes: ground, input shaft with its inclined journal, the trunnion ring, the output shaft with its yoke; a spherical four-bar, the four revolute axes (input shaft, journal, trunnions, output shaft) meeting at one centre. The kin block keeps the journal sleeve pinned on the input and the arm keyed on the output as bodies of their own (posed with them), so the joint count does not give the mobility: Kutzbach counts 5, which ignores the concurrent axes and counts the sleeve's spin; the true mobility is 1, solved in closed form by the spherical-four-bar block. The loop is overconstrained in the count, as a universal joint is.

explain.motion: The input shaft carries a journal set at a small angle α to its axis, and a ring turns on the journal in bearings. Trunnion pins on the ring, square to the journal, sit in a yoke on an output shaft that stands square to the input. All four axes meet at one centre, so the ring cannot turn with the shaft: it nods, and the yoke rocks the output to and fro through exactly ±α while the input turns on. The swing follows ψ = atan(tan α sin θ), close to a sine, and an arm on the output turns it into a stroke of 2 L sin α.
explain.forces: The input torque reaches the output as a pair of forces on the trunnions, carried by the ring's bearings on the journal. The output moves fastest, at tan α times the input speed, as it passes mid-swing, and its reaction then twists the journal hardest; at the ends of the swing it stands still and a load on the arm cannot turn the input.
explain.benefits: It turns a fast shaft into a strong, smooth, nearly sinusoidal rocking in a compact sealed unit, with only turning bearings and no sliding guides.
explain.limits: The swing is fixed by the journal's angle, so changing the stroke means a new journal. The axes must meet at one point: a machining or shimming error loads the bearings and wears them quickly, and the rocking mass shakes the frame at high speed.

build.ground: base plate with the input shaft's two pillow blocks and the output shaft's, the two axes square and meeting at the centre
build.defining_relations: spherical four-bar with input link α (journal to shaft), coupler 90° (journal to trunnions), output link 90° (trunnions to output shaft), ground 90° (input to output); output angle ψ = atan(tan α sin θ), θ from the pose where the journal leans in the plane of the two shafts (equivalently ψ = atan(tan α cos θ) counted from the pose square to it); amplitude exactly α; output speed ratio dψ/dθ = tan α cos θ / (1 + tan²α sin²θ), at most tan α; arm stroke 2 L sin α
build.notes: Input 360° continuous; the output rocks ±15° at α = 15° and a 60 mm arm sweeps a chord of 31.1 mm. Every axis must pass through the centre. The ring's bearings on the journal take the trunnion loads; the trunnions turn in needle cups in the yoke's arms. At θ = 0 the journal leans in the plane of the two shafts, the trunnions stand upright and the yoke and arm are at mid-swing.

review.note: T2 before the build, from the solved kinematics: six phases at 60 degrees of input give swings of 0, -13.1, -13.1, 0, +13.1, +13.1 degrees, so the yoke and the arm visibly rock while the shaft turns; the solve matches psi = atan(tan(alpha) sin(theta)) to 2e-14 at 8, 15 and 25 degrees, amplitude exactly alpha, within 0.13 degrees of a pure sine at 15; the arm tip sweeps 31.1 mm; the output's speed ratio peaks at tan(alpha) at mid-swing; no dwell. Decided: the output shaft lies in plan square to the input, as the universal joint's does, so the two relatives read side by side; the reference pose is mid-swing (journal leaning in the plane of the two shafts, trunnions upright, yoke and arm upright), so the journal angle reads true in PLAN at the start; the journal angle is a control (5 to 25 degrees) with a ghost trace and plot ghosts at 8 and 25, because 'the swing is the journal's angle' is the lesson; the arm's tip is traced with equal-time ticks every 15 degrees (bunched at the ends of the stroke, near harmonic) and a rim point of the ring is traced to show its nod; construction: the four axis lines (input, journal, trunnion, output) and a circle at the common centre, the journal angle arc, the stroke dimension; default view ISOMETRIC, where all four axes and the nod read at once; section A-A through the input and journal axes at the start shows the inclined journal inside the ring on its bearings, the one part of the principle a housing hides; no use context in the drawing.
